questions.q: What did the marshmallow experiment show about children who delayed gratification?
a: They tended to have better lives later on
They were more likely to become overweight
They achieved less in school than their peers
They became impatient adults
questions.why: The overview says follow-up studies found the children who waited for the second marshmallow fared better in life.

questions.q: What does Joe De Sena recommend doing to force yourself to take on a challenge?
a: Sign up for an event in advance and commit to a plan
Wait until you feel fully ready to begin
Keep your goal private so no one can see you fail
Start with the hardest possible challenge first
questions.why: The overview says committing to a dated event makes you accountable and honest about following through.

questions.q: Why include other people in your plan, according to the summary?
a: They keep you accountable and may support you
They can train for the event on your behalf
They make the challenge easier to complete
They can pay part of the entry fee
questions.why: The overview advises telling others about your plan so they hold you to it, including quieter supporters.

questions.q: What advice does the summary give about diet?
a: Ignore most modern diets and eat simple, plainly healthy food
Follow a strict calorie count every single day
Try a new popular diet each month
Skip breakfast to strengthen willpower
questions.why: The overview recommends simple categories of healthy food such as nuts, vegetables and fruit.

questions.q: What does “stoic calm” mean in the summary?
a: Keeping your temper and focusing only on what you control
Suppressing every emotion until you feel nothing
Avoiding every situation you cannot predict
Accepting that effort makes no difference
questions.why: The overview defines stoic calm as not losing your temper and concentrating on what is within your control.
